name: Create Your Exquisite Monsters
description:
How playful can a monster be? 
This storytelling session introduces children and parents to Monsters of my Mind,  a book that explores art and expression. Through a collaborative drawing activity, children create their own monsters, and explore what their personalities might be. The monster may look funny, awkward, confusing or strange. Feelings can be like that too. But when given shape, they can be looked at with curiosity instead of fear, becoming something we can understand. 
The session aims to introduce children to the power of artistic expression and start a conversation about understanding feelings, all while providing plenty of laughs and giggles! 
Around the World in 50 Sundays is a journey that begins, not with a ticket, but with opening a book. In a city like Bangalore where families are always in motion, the BIC Library hopes to offer stillness and a quiet, welcoming space for both parents and children where reading becomes a shared experience. Every Sunday, we open our doors to invite you into a library that listens; building a rhythm of return, a habit of joy and a new community bound not just by books, but by the weekly ritual of reading together.  
We welcome your ideas and input. If you have suggestions for children’s events or activities that align with this vision, we’d love to hear from you. Please reach out to us at library@bangaloreinternationalcentre.org

name: Health, Heritage and Architecture
description:
This hands-on workshop uses real drawings of Rajasthan’s forts and palaces to show how centuries-old builders kept rooms cool, airy, bright, and quiet without electricity or any energy-dependent mechanisms. Participants read walls, courtyards, and openings as the working parts of a healthy building, and learn how the spaces we live in shape our health and learning. Along the way, participants discover the role architects play in designing healthier spaces, and what it takes to bring that old intelligence into new rooms. What might those builders teach the architects of today? 
This event is a part of the “Drawing Knowledge” exhibition, exploring the intelligent architecture of imperial India. Find the full schedule here.

name: The Nation Wants to Know
description:
From Mumbai to New York, laughter truly needs no visa! 
This fast-paced, razor-sharp comedic journeys through the quirks of modern India, and how they echo with (or utterly confuse) audiences across the globe. With a signature blend of wit, warmth, and wild storytelling, the topics move from the absurdities of colonial hangovers to the chaotic charm of startups, social media spats, and airline adventures. 
After sold-out performances world over, the show brings back international tales, asking what happens when India’s inside jokes meet the world’s outside gaze?

name: SamaBhav International Travelling Film Festival
description:
SamaBhav, meaning equanimity, is a two-day film festival on gender, identity, sexuality, and social change. Screenings of curated short, documentary, and feature films are interspersed with conversations with filmmakers, protagonists, activists, and experts. How often do we get a room where these questions can be asked openly? 
Now in its eighth edition, the festival travels to cities and districts across India and beyond, reaching young people and their educators. Curated by Men Against Violence and Abuse (MAVA), the films address gender-based discrimination and violence, patriarchy, misogyny, homophobia, transphobia, and the meaning of masculinity. The discussions that follow invite audiences to examine their own biases and prejudices, in a safe space for young men, young women, and non-binary youth to speak about subjects rarely raised in classrooms or at home.

name: Before the Blueprint
description:
Where did the people living in the palaces get water from? What do the thick walls mean? And why are there so many courtyards? 
This workshop brings participants and students of architecture together around a table to read drawings of Rajasthan’s forts and palaces. Through writing and sketching, participants will uncover what these iconic buildings know about climate, water, and defence. 
Drawings are how architecture speaks to society, a shared language of abstraction that clients, builders, and architects rely on. Yet the great forts rose without them, shaped by craftspeople whose skill lived in practice rather than on paper. Participants learn to read that knowledge back out of walls, courtyards, and water systems, one sketch at a time. 
Please Note: 

Participants should bring a notebook, pen, pencil and eraser.
Limited to 30 spots.

name: Beyond the Lines
description:
This panel discussion reads the drawings of Rajasthan’s forts and palaces as an archive, asking what role they might play in future scholarship. Placed together, the detailed works in the exhibition reveal spatial intricacies, the persistence of architectural elements across centuries, and the material intelligence of the craftspeople who built them. The panel sifts through their possible interpretations to draw out the tacit knowledge, socio-cultural practices, political structures, and physical environments embedded in the drawings.

name: Rare Ritual Performances of Keralam
description:
This illustrated lecture explores the ritual performances of northern Keralam. Beyond Theyyam, more than a hundred such performances are still practised, largely unknown outside their regions. Art, martial practices and shared worship have long held communities together and this talk presents a visual record of the rare traditions that preserve Keralam’s cultural identity. 
Balan Nambiar returns to BIC, where he last spoke on the Bhutas of Tulunadu, with his lens focused on a different region. He presents photographs of traditions that developed alongside, and often independently of, Brahmanical Hinduism. He looks at Ati, a ritual of bare-handed combat at Mavilayi influenced by Kalaripayattu, and at shrines where Muslim Theyyams enjoy patronage and privileges. He captures offerings of toddy, fish, and meat as expressions of local belief, and introduces lesser-known forms such as Uccerikuttu, Malayankettu, and Kalampattu, now seldom performed. He makes the case that preservation of these practices is essential to safeguarding the region’s cultural heritage. 
This talk is part of a series marking twenty years of BIC.

name: Paswaar
description:
39 min | Gujarati and Hindi with English Subtitles | India | 2025 
One of the few surviving Zoroastrians in the world, Dr. Homi is rich in inheritance but devoid of children. His only kin is his estranged nephew Jamshed. In the vast emptiness of his huge mansion, his young caregiver and cook, Lali, brings the warmth of a home with her tender, motherly love. On the day of Homi’s birthday, as Lali passionately cooks a Parsi feast of fish and vermicelli, Homi longingly waits for Jamshed to pay him a visit. As he considers who should inherit his estate, the film explores an unlikely bond shaped by loneliness, affection, belonging, and the human need for care. Will Homi finally acknowledge the value Lali brings to his lonely life? 
The filmmaker will be present for a Q&A post the screening.

name: Making of an Identity
description:
What is hidden in the meal, woven into the cloth? 
This talk explores the stories behind what we eat and what we wear, tracing how everyday cultural practices carry the marks of migration, trade, technology, politics, identity, and the exchange of ideas across the Indian subcontinent. Through historical anecdotes and conversation, it treats food and clothing not as markers of tradition alone, but as living records of a history that continues to be written today. Drawing from the book The Music of Stones, the session invites the audience to look at the most familiar parts of daily life with fresh curiosity. 
This talk is part of “Karwaan Baithak,” Karwaan Heritage’s public lecture and dialogue series.

name: Drawing Knowledge
description:
What can we learn about place and people from a detailed drawing? 
This exhibition presents one of the largest private collections of architectural drawings of Rajasthan’s forts and palaces, from Jaisalmer and Amber to Mehrangarh and Hawa Mahal. Each drawing is the product of years of research and meticulous documentation, recording the walls, courtyards, and water systems that shaped life inside these buildings. 
Comprehensive documentation of such places is increasingly scarce. Made possible by the mentorship of Kulbhushan Jain and Minakshi Jain, the collection brings this accumulated knowledge into the public domain. It gives researchers, students, and curious visitors access to study the details closely, now and for generations to come.

name: Giving Shape to the Inner World
description:
This evening explores how giving a feeling a shape, as a character, an image, or a letter, can help us understand our inner worlds. Based on the book Monsters of My Mind, the session moves between conversation and hands-on making, asking how creativity can help us say what words alone cannot. What would your monster look like? 
Members of the panel read scenes from the book, opening a conversation on how comics, humour, and absurdity make difficult experiences easier to look at. Inspired by Leonora Carrington’s Surrealist Survival Kit, postcards are shared, with five prompts: courage, joy, adventure, love, and possibility. The evening closes with a short letter to a monster of your own, with no need to name or explain it. That which feels deeply personal, need not be isolating.

name: The Sitar’s Journey in Melody
description:
An immersive morning of sitar and tabla awaits. 
This Hindustani classical concert offers a unique exploration of the instrument that stands as the backbone of the tradition: the sitar. It begins with a lecture-demonstration tracing historical roots, structural design, tonal acoustics, and stylistic transformations over centuries. Following this is a full morning raga recital, highlighting the rich aesthetic traditions and intricate rhythmic dialogues between sitar and tabla. 
For both the seasoned connoisseurs and new listeners, this session offers a deeper appreciation of the heritage, craft, and soul of Indian classical music. The sitar is not just a musical instrument, but a living, evolving canvas of Indian culture that bridges centuries of tradition with timeless acoustic mastery.
